lessons.title: Nutrient Requirements for Layers at Different Stages
lessons.body: Layers need different nutrients as they grow. From day-old to 6 weeks (brooding), feed them chick starter mash with 20% protein. This builds strong bones and organs. From 7 to 18 weeks (growing), switch to grower mash with 16% protein. This stage prepares them for laying without making them too fat. At 18 weeks, move to layer mash with 16-18% protein and 3.5-4.5% calcium. Calcium is critical for eggshells. A hen laying 5 eggs per week needs about 4 grams of calcium daily. If you see thin or soft shells, increase calcium. Energy comes from maize, millet, or sorghum. A layer needs about 2800-3000 kcal per kg of feed. Too little energy means fewer eggs. Too much makes them fat and stops laying. Protein is for egg white and body repair. Use soybean meal, fishmeal, or groundnut cake. Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts. A lack of vitamin A causes weak chicks; vitamin D3 helps calcium absorption. Always provide clean water. A hen drinks 250-500 ml per day. Without water, she stops eating. In hot weather, add electrolytes. For 100 hens, you need about 12-15 kg of feed per day. Adjust based on how much they eat. Weigh a sample of eggs monthly. If egg size drops, check protein and energy. Keep records of feed intake and egg production. This helps you spot problems early.

lessons.title: Types of Feed: Mash, Pellets, and Crumbs
lessons.body: Feeds come in three forms: mash, pellets, and crumbs. Mash is ground feed, like coarse flour. It is the cheapest and easiest to make on-farm. You can mix your own ingredients. But hens waste some mash by billing it out. To reduce waste, feed in troughs and do not fill more than half full. Pellets are mash pressed into small sticks. Hens eat pellets faster and waste less. Pellets also prevent selective eatingâhens cannot pick out only maize. This means they get a balanced diet. Pellets cost more because of processing. Crumbs are broken pellets, used for chicks. They are easier for small beaks. For layers, you can use mash or pellets. In Africa, many farmers use mash because it is affordable. If you make your own mash, grind ingredients to medium textureânot too fine, or it becomes dusty. A hammer mill with a 3-5 mm screen works well. Store feed in dry, ventilated bags. Never use mouldy feed. Moulds produce aflatoxins that kill hens and lower egg production. If you buy commercial feed, check the label for protein, fat, fibre, and calcium. Good layer mash has 16-18% protein, 3.5-4.5% calcium, and 0.5% phosphorus. Pellets should be 3-4 mm diameter. Crumbs are 1-2 mm. Use pellets in rainy season when mash gets sticky. Always provide grit (small stones) with mash to help digestion. Grit stays in the gizzard and grinds food. Without grit, mash passes undigested. You can buy granite grit or use clean river sand. Offer 1 kg of grit per 100 hens per week.

lessons.title: Formulating Balanced Rations with Local Ingredients
lessons.body: You can mix your own layer feed using local ingredients. A balanced ration has energy, protein, minerals, and vitamins. For 100 kg of layer mash, use: 55 kg maize (energy), 20 kg soybean meal (protein), 10 kg fishmeal (protein and minerals), 8 kg wheat bran or rice bran (fibre and energy), 5 kg limestone or oyster shell (calcium), 1 kg bone meal (phosphorus), 0.5 kg salt, and 0.5 kg vitamin-mineral premix. This gives about 17% protein and 4% calcium. If soybean meal is expensive, use 15 kg soybean meal and 5 kg groundnut cake. But groundnut cake can have aflatoxinâtest it or buy from trusted sellers. Fishmeal should be 60-65% protein. Local fishmeal from small dried fish works if ground well. Maize can be replaced with millet, sorghum, or cassava chips. If using cassava, add 0.2% methionine because cassava lacks this amino acid. Mix all ingredients thoroughly on a clean concrete floor. Use a shovel to turn the pile 3 times. Store in clean bags. Make only what you will use in 2 weeks to avoid mould. For 100 hens, you need about 12 kg per day. So 100 kg lasts about 8 days. Weigh ingredients with a scaleâdo not guess. A 50 kg scale is enough. Keep a notebook of your formula and how hens respond. If egg production drops, adjust protein or energy. Always provide clean water and grit. This ration works for layers from 18 weeks onwards. For chicks and growers, adjust protein and calcium: chicks need 20% protein and 1% calcium; growers need 16% protein and 1% calcium.

lessons.title: Feeding Schedules and Feed Management
lessons.body: Layers eat best when fed at the same times daily. Give them two main meals: one in the morning (7-8 am) and one in the afternoon (3-4 pm). This matches their natural eating pattern. In hot climates, feed early and late to avoid the heat of the day. Hens eat less when it is hot. If you feed only once, they may overeat and waste. For 100 hens, give about 6 kg in the morning and 6 kg in the afternoon. Adjust based on how much they leave. If feed is left after 30 minutes, reduce the next meal. Always provide clean water. A hen drinks up to 500 ml daily. In hot weather, she may drink double. Water should be cool and clean. Use drinkers that are easy to clean. Feed in troughs that allow all hens to eat at once. Allow 10-12 cm of trough space per hen. For 100 hens, you need 10-12 meters of trough. If troughs are too short, strong hens eat more and weak ones starve. Clean troughs daily to remove old feed. Old feed can grow mould. Store feed in a dry, dark room on pallets. Keep bags off the floor and away from walls. Use oldest feed first. Never mix new feed with old. Weigh a sample of hens monthly to check body condition. A layer should weigh 1.8-2.2 kg. If they are too thin, increase feed. If too fat, reduce energy. Keep records of feed used and eggs collected. This helps you calculate feed conversion ratio (FCR). Good FCR for layers is 2.0-2.5 kg feed per kg eggs. If FCR is high, check for disease or feed waste.

lessons.title: Supplements: Vitamins, Minerals, and Grit
lessons.body: Even with a good ration, layers may need supplements. Vitamins are needed for health and egg production. Vitamin A for eyes and immunity, vitamin D3 for calcium absorption, vitamin E for fertility and hatchability. A lack of vitamin D3 causes soft-shelled eggs. You can buy commercial vitamin premixes. Add 0.5 kg per 100 kg of feed. If hens are on deep litter and get sunlight, they make vitamin D themselves. But in cloudy weather, supplement. Minerals: calcium and phosphorus are the most important. Calcium for eggshells, phosphorus for bones. The ratio should be 2:1 calcium to phosphorus. If you use limestone and bone meal, you are covered. But if you see thin shells, add oyster shell free-choice. Offer it in a separate feeder. Hens will eat what they need. Grit is small stones that help grind feed in the gizzard. Without grit, feed passes undigested. Use granite grit or clean river sand. Give 1 kg per 100 hens per week. Sprinkle on feed or offer separately. Salt is needed but in small amounts. 0.5 kg per 100 kg feed. Too much salt causes water belly and death. Do not add extra salt if your premix already has some. Other supplements: probiotics for gut health, toxins binders if feed may have mould. In Africa, many farmers use local herbs like aloe vera or garlic as supplements. These can help but are not a substitute for balanced feed. Always follow label instructions. Overdosing vitamins can be toxic. Store supplements in cool, dry place. Mix only what you will use in one week. Keep records of what you add and when.

lessons.title: Avoiding Feed Waste and Contamination
lessons.body: Feed is your biggest cost. Waste and contamination cut your profit. To avoid waste: use proper feeders. Troughs should be deep enough so hens cannot bill feed out. Fill only half full. If feeders are too full, hens scoop feed onto the floor. For 100 hens, use 10-12 meters of trough. Feed at fixed times. Do not leave feed in troughs all day. Remove leftover feed after 30 minutes. Store feed in clean, dry bags on pallets. Keep bags off the floor and away from walls. Use oldest feed first. Never mix new feed with old. Protect feed from rodents and birds. They eat feed and spread disease. Use metal bins with tight lids. For contamination: never use mouldy feed. Moulds produce aflatoxins that damage the liver and lower egg production. If feed smells musty or has green spots, throw it away. Do not feed it to hens. Keep water clean. Dirty water can spread disease. Clean drinkers daily. Do not let hens walk in feed. Use feeders that prevent them from standing in feed. If you make your own feed, use clean equipment. Do not mix on dirty floors. Store ingredients separately. Check for insects. If you see weevils, sun-dry the grain or use food-grade diatomaceous earth. Never use pesticides on feed. Keep a record of feed bought and used. This helps you spot waste. A good layer farm loses less than 5% of feed. If you lose more, check feeders and storage. Also, watch for feed theft by workers or animals. Lock feed store. Weigh feed before and after. If you see sudden drop in feed use but eggs are same, check for waste. Healthy hens, clean feed, clean waterâthese are the keys to profit.

quiz.q: What is the recommended protein level for layer mash?
quiz.explanation: Layer mash should have 16-18% protein to support egg production.

quiz.q: At what age should you switch from grower mash to layer mash?
quiz.explanation: Layers start laying around 18 weeks, so they need layer mash from then.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is most critical for strong eggshells?
quiz.explanation: Calcium is the main mineral in eggshells; a lack causes thin or soft shells.

quiz.q: How much water does a laying hen drink per day?
quiz.explanation: A hen drinks about 250-500 ml daily, more in hot weather.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of pellets over mash?
options: D) They are easier to make
quiz.explanation: Pellets prevent selective eating and billing out, so less feed is wasted.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid mouldy feed?
options: D) It has too much protein
quiz.explanation: Mouldy feed contains aflatoxins that damage the liver and reduce egg production.

quiz.q: What is the recommended calcium level in layer mash?
quiz.explanation: Layer mash should have 3.5-4.5% calcium for strong eggshells.

quiz.q: Which local ingredient is a good source of protein?
quiz.explanation: Soybean meal is high in protein (about 44-48%) and commonly used in layer rations.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of grit in poultry feed?
options: B) Helps grind feed in the gizzard
quiz.explanation: Grit stays in the gizzard and helps grind feed for better digestion.

quiz.q: How much grit should you provide per 100 hens per week?
quiz.explanation: Offer about 1 kg of grit per 100 hens per week.

quiz.q: What is a good feed conversion ratio (FCR) for layers?
quiz.explanation: Good layers convert 2.0-2.5 kg of feed into 1 kg of eggs.

quiz.q: How often should you feed layers?
quiz.explanation: Feeding twice daily (morning and afternoon) matches natural eating patterns and reduces waste.

quiz.q: What is the recommended trough space per hen?
quiz.explanation: Allow 10-12 cm of trough space per hen so all can eat at once.

quiz.q: Which vitamin is needed for calcium absorption?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin D3 helps the hen absorb calcium from the gut.

quiz.q: What is the ideal calcium to phosphorus ratio in layer feed?
quiz.explanation: A 2:1 calcium to phosphorus ratio is ideal for bone health and eggshell formation.

quiz.q: What can you use as a local calcium source?
quiz.explanation: Oyster shell is a good source of calcium and can be offered free-choice.

quiz.q: How should you store feed to prevent contamination?
options: C) On pallets in a dry room
quiz.explanation: Store feed on pallets in a dry, dark room to prevent moisture and mould.

quiz.q: What is a sign of feed waste?
options: B) Feed left in troughs after 30 minutes
quiz.explanation: Leftover feed after 30 minutes indicates overfeeding or feeder design problems.

quiz.q: Which supplement can help if feed may have mould?
quiz.explanation: Toxin binders help reduce the harmful effects of aflatoxins in feed.

quiz.q: What is the maximum salt level in layer feed?
quiz.explanation: Salt should not exceed 0.5% in the total ration to avoid toxicity.

quiz.q: Why should you not mix new feed with old feed?
quiz.explanation: Mixing can introduce moisture and mould from old feed to new feed.

quiz.q: What is the best way to prevent rodents from eating feed?
options: A) Use metal bins with tight lids
B) Leave feed in open bags
quiz.explanation: Metal bins with tight lids keep rodents out and protect feed.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of aflatoxin poisoning?
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxins damage the liver and cause a drop in egg production.

quiz.q: How much feed does a layer eat per day?
quiz.explanation: A layer eats about 100-120 g of feed per day, depending on weather and production.

quiz.q: What is the ideal body weight for a layer hen?
quiz.explanation: A healthy layer should weigh 1.8-2.2 kg; too thin or too fat reduces laying.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see thin eggshells?
quiz.explanation: Thin shells indicate a calcium deficiency; add limestone or oyster shell.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good energy source for layer feed?
quiz.explanation: Maize is the main energy source in most African layer rations.

quiz.q: How often should you clean feed troughs?
quiz.explanation: Clean troughs daily to remove old feed and prevent mould growth.

quiz.q: What is the recommended vitamin-mineral premix inclusion rate?
quiz.explanation: Add 0.5 kg of vitamin-mineral premix per 100 kg of feed.

quiz.q: What is a good practice to reduce feed waste?
options: A) Fill feeders to the top
quiz.explanation: Feeding at fixed times prevents overfeeding and reduces waste.
